contents:
Afternoon, the 3rd day of Snowen, 1525.

Today turned out… productive. After long years, a vial of pure blood of a member of the D’Aloray dynasty has at last come into my possession. Florimond, a cousin of Alexandrine D’Aloray, was forced into flight during the struggle for the throne, and for a long while dwelt in the port city of Villefugiou. Though he managed to dissolve into the common crowd, by a lucky turn of circumstance he was identified and detained by our troops during the seizure of the city and the nearby region that followed our company’s successful landing. He looked more like a well-to-do merchant than a member of the royal family. However, one of the soldiers had his attention caught by the pendant at his neck, noticed at the moment of arrest, when he was trying to flee from the city after the siege began. The pendant bore royal heraldry, and inside was a miniature depicting, presumably, his mother. Odd that he simply forgot to take it off. Presumably he faltered and, in his haste, grabbed whatever he could carry off. He was brought to me without delay, and thereafter we took him captive. Yesterday he was sent on to the capital, since such a “find” really is a rare treasure, but before that I managed to take blood samples from him in a permissible volume.

I would rather Hnat did not learn of my unsanctioned experiments. It may be wrong of me to occupy myself with such things alone, without general disclosure, but neither he nor the Major would plainly approve of that sort of activity. The original series of studies was shut down on account of the spontaneity and ambiguity of the results. Hnat is an understanding man, and one with a large heart: he would not encourage any further risks to my health, all the more so, in his view, without weighty reason, since he lost his faith in blood infusions after the closure. I see no sense in stirring him up over this. At the moment he is meticulously studying the flora of the vampire forest, resting from all of this, so it is definitely not worth troubling him with the news that I am back to my old pursuit again. Besides, though he has not yet reported any concrete results, he let slip that he had arrived at something new and asked not to be distracted.

As soon as I was free of other concerns, I set about creating the serum. It took me half a day all told, but the resulting solution came out rather pure. The blood itself, in its shade, calls to mind the juice of a blood orange, only a little yellower, perhaps. A peculiar description, I agree, but as an alchemist I am far too taken with the consistency and the hue of this blood; I cannot tear my eyes from it. It certainly has a better chance of yielding an agreeable result than ordinary pure blood does. Say what you will, this blood is of nearly the highest purity — it is not the blood of some dummy barons. Although the results of Hnat’s and my research were written off as accidental, I still hold to the opinion that the outcome depended first and foremost on the purity of the blood and, no less importantly, on the “maturity” of the hunter. To be more precise, on the maturity of his malora, as I explain it, or, put plainly, on his experience as a hunter. Statistically, the stronger the subject was, the more favourable the effects turned out to be, though in most cases inconstant. I also have the impression that susceptibility to blood infusion depends as well on the patient’s character, but unfortunately, I cannot peer into everyone’s soul, so there is no proving it — nor, for that matter, disproving it. In the others’ opinion there were no patterns at all, and we were simply jabbing people for the sake of unpredictable effects, both good and less so. More experienced hunters very rarely volunteered, which is why the sample for them is smaller than for the cadets, and so in the overall tally it looks as though infusions bring more trouble than benefit. But obviously, seeing those figures, they would not have risked allotting us more qualified hunters.

I introduced the serum into myself about an hour ago, before sitting down to the diary, but so far, I have noticed nothing in particular. Tomorrow, with a clear head, I shall set it all down in detail.

Evening, the 4th day of Snowen, 1525.

All the observations I shall write out in more detail in a separate document, and here I will probably just lay out the general impression. Though, knowing myself, I shall in the end most likely spend considerably more pages setting all this out than I originally planned. In truth the royal blood has gladdened me: a great deal of interest all at once; as for usefulness, that is a separate matter, but I have noticed no purely negative consequences so far, which cannot but please me, even though there are a few questionable ones. Listed here is what I managed to discover in a bit more than a day; it is entirely possible the list is incomplete — I cannot know for sure.

I should like to begin with vision, since that is perhaps the most palpable change. My eyes adapt almost instantly to the absence of light, and I can also make out objects in pitch darkness far more distinctly. The shape of an object is visible, its position, but the contrast between different surfaces is practically imperceptible. On top of that, telling colours apart is impossible in the fullest sense of the word. I presume that if vampires do not see in exactly this way, then in a similar way. There is, however, one significant drawback to all of this: in the light it goes unnoticed, but in darkness it is plain to see that my eyes glow. It is not a reflection, as with ordinary animals, but precisely a visual burning in the dark, as with vampires. Praise the heavens, I have not acquired crimson irises, or anything worse, otherwise it would have caused problems of a certain kind: my eyes have remained the same sapphire blue as before. In the field the ability to see in the dark will definitely be useful, but the glow of the eyes will make me more noticeable from a distance, and I will have to explain to very nearly everyone why my eyes are glowing. A pity that making passive night vision more widespread does not yet seem possible. Once I grow used to it, I shall no longer be able to imagine living without it.

The following may be taken with a measure of scepticism, simply because of the short span of time available for tests, but I am inclined to believe that it has become easier for my body to recover from wounds. I noticed that soon after the infusion some of my scars faded and my skin became smoother and clearer, though not pale. This, moreover, may be not so much passive regeneration as a surge of it, rather like vampires after the ritual of blood cleansing, or else an infusion, on whose principle our own blood infusions are founded. Nevertheless, I decided to measure the regeneration by making an incision on my left arm. Hunters already need less time for wounds to close than ordinary people do: a cut of this sort would have healed on me in about two days. Here it took roughly a day. Again, the information is approximate, and any number of factors could have influenced the result, but I can state for certain that the speed of my regeneration has increased — the only question is by how much. By my own sense of it, at least half again to twice as fast. Measuring it in the middle of a fight, incidentally, is not something one could really manage. In such conditions it is foolish not to use healing potions, which obviously accelerate the closing of wounds and therefore affect the result. The only real option is to cut myself repeatedly, but for now I have other things to occupy myself with. I shall come back to it sometime later.

It was obvious that the infusion could in one form or another affect my feeding, so I tested everything I could with regard to food. With ordinary food I noticed no difference: in smell, in taste, in appearance — all the same. However, I resolved to check my reaction to animal and human blood: I had an idea who to “borrow” it from, so no difficulties arose. I can put it this way: I began to sense a slight sweetness both in the smell and in the taste. In taste, cow blood took on a faint hint of meat as though in cranberry sauce. Faint, but perceptible. Human blood put me in mind of marzipan somehow — I do not know exactly why. I had heated up the blood beforehand, whisking it in the process to steer clear of clotting, which ought to have disinfected it, on account of which it may either have lost its taste or acquired one that was not there in the blood originally. I hope the taste was more or less preserved, since I do not intend to try it as it is: catching some disease on top of everything else is the last thing I need. I drank a litre or so of it, trying to describe the taste to myself more precisely; I would not say it came out well — nothing similar comes to mind. For what it's worth, I have not become a bloodsucker on account of it: I have no desire to bite anyone. It is worth mentioning that the blood of vampires themselves has grown more repellent to me than before: its taste now seems more earthy, if anything. Yes, I had tried it before as well, apart from the infusions: it was simply like blood, only muddier. The one thing — I am not sure this interest in blood will lead me to anything genuinely useful. I had an idea of trying blood wine for variety’s sake, but I have no recipe for its preparation, so I shall simply grab a bottle to try during some raid or other.
